nodes.text: Applying AM-GM to denominators 1+b≥2√b gives an upper bound 1/(a(1+b)) ≤ 1/(2a√b), which is the wrong direction for proving a lower bound.
Scaling by t=1/(abc)^(1/3) so that a' b' c' = 1 fails to directly connect to the original, because scaling changes 1+b to 1+bt, not preserving the inequality form.
Using Cauchy-Schwarz (Σ1/(a(1+b)))(Σ a(1+b)) ≥ 9 and trying to prove Σ a(1+b) ≤ 3(1+abc) fails: a counterexample a=2,b=2,c=0.25 gives LHS=9.25, RHS=6, disproving the needed inequality.
AM-GM on the transformed form Σ xy/(y+1) leads to needing to prove (x+1)(y+1)(z+1) ≤ (k+1)³/k, which is a complicated inequality without an obvious proof.

Claiming 'by scaling, it extends to the general case' without showing the actual transformation is insufficient — the scaling must preserve the inequality's structure, and this must be verified explicitly
Naively substituting a = 1/x, b = 1/y, c = 1/z does not help because it only rewrites abc = 1 as (1/xyz) = 1, introducing no simplification

Applying the standard Cauchy-Schwarz (∑ a_i b_i)² ≤ (∑ a_i²)(∑ b_i²) gives an upper bound, not helpful for proving a sum is ≥ something; the Engel form ∑ a_i²/b_i ≥ (∑ a_i)²/(∑ b_i) is needed for lower bounds

Naively applying Engel without first putting each term into the exact a_i²/b_i form (e.g., treating yz/(x(y+z)) as a_i²/b_i without squaring the numerator) misapplies the inequality and gives an incorrect bound
Applying AM-GM directly to an expression containing negative terms gives a wrong bound because the inequality reverses or is invalid
Using AM-GM to claim a minimum without verifying the equality condition is achievable leaves the bound unattained — the true minimum may be higher
Applying AM-GM to maximize a sum or minimize a product reverses the intended inequality direction
Naïvely applying y+z ≥ 2√(yz) gives yz/(x(y+z)) ≤ √(yz)/(2x), an upper bound — the opposite direction needed for a lower-bound proof.
Trying to prove each individual term yz/(x(y+z)) ≥ something fails; the bound holds only for the cyclic sum as a whole.
Dividing each variable by k (power 1) instead of k^{1/3}, which would not cancel the triple product to 1
Applying k^{-1/3} scaling without requiring a,b,c > 0 — if any were zero, k = 0 and the scaling factor is undefined
Assuming a'b'c' = 1 forces a' = b' = c' = 1, ignoring that infinitely many triples multiply to 1
Trying to directly manipulate abc = 1 in an inequality without substitution often leads to messy expansions that obscure the underlying symmetry.
Claiming yz/(x(y+z)) ≥ √(yz)/(2x) from AM-GM reverses the inequality: a lower bound on a positive denominator produces an upper bound on the fraction, not a lower bound
Applying AM-GM directly to a single term yz/(x(y+z)) or to the sum without the ½(∑√(yz)/x) intermediate step does not yield the desired constant 3/2
Working directly with unnormalized variables (a,b,c) often leads to messy expressions without the product=1 simplification
Using y+z >= 2sqrt(yz) to claim yz/(x(y+z)) >= sqrt(yz)/(2x) reverses the inequality.
The attempted abc=1 proof based on the reversed denominator bound is invalid.
Normalizing abc to 1 by common scaling does not directly prove the original non-homogeneous inequality.
Applying Cauchy-Schwarz here fails if it relies on the false upper bound sum a(1+b) <= 3(1+abc).
The general cyclic product parametrization creates a more complicated inequality without an immediate proof.
The reciprocal AM-GM bound leaves an unproved condition on (x+1)(y+1)(z+1).
The substitution a=x/y, b=y/z, c=z/x only covers triples with abc=1.
Treating a normalized proof plus an unstated scaling argument as a complete proof is insufficient when the general-case scaling step has not been articulated.
Using AM-GM to claim yz/(x(y + z)) >= sqrt(yz)/(2x) reverses the inequality direction.
A common mistake is to use y + z >= 2 sqrt(yz) and then keep the same inequality direction after taking reciprocals.
It is a pitfall to infer sum yz/(x(y+z)) >= 1/2 sum of the radical-ratio terms; the natural AM-GM termwise comparison has the opposite direction.
Assuming two triangles with the same incenter must have the same incircle is wrong because the inradius can differ.
Forcing the distance from the shared incenter to EF to equal ABC's inradius incorrectly assumes the two triangles have the same inradius.
Concluding EF must equal AB from the shared-incenter condition follows from the false same-incircle assumption.
Reducing the problem to EF = AB makes the proof trivial but does not address the intended nontrivial configuration.
Assuming a different line through D can preserve the same incenter is a wrong approach.
Do not treat one entry as satisfying both the factor 5 and factor 2 requirements in this range.
Counting triples with at least one 5 alone is insufficient because some of those triples have no even entry.
It is wrong to let the same entry satisfy both the 5 requirement and the even requirement because 5 is not even.
Including the exactly-three-5s case as valid is wrong because that case has no even entry.
Treating a triple of three 5s as satisfying the even-number condition is wrong because 5 is odd.
Directly assigning positions for required values can overcount triples when extra positions may repeat required values.
After fixing one 5, counting all remaining non-5 pairs is wrong because the triple still needs an even entry.
Accepting 11 without checking its remainder modulo 7 is wrong because the remainder is 4, which is not square-free.
Requiring all remaining checks after a candidate has already failed one required condition is unnecessary.
A common mistake is to accept p merely because p is prime without checking remainders modulo all smaller primes.
A common mistake is to keep p when most remainders are square-free even though one checked remainder is not square-free.
Treating a candidate as valid after finding remainder 4 is wrong because 4 contains the square factor 2 squared.
Declaring p=13 valid after checking only its remainder modulo 11 is incomplete.
Continuing to test a candidate after a disqualifying modulo-5 remainder wastes work because the candidate is already eliminated.
Do not infer from a few examples that all primes larger than 13 fail without a proof or exhaustive check.
Checking only whether a remainder is a perfect square is insufficient because non-square numbers can still have square factors.
Using p-1 being square-free as the criterion is wrong because other remainders p mod q can fail.
Treating 4 as square-free is wrong because it contains the repeated prime factor 2.
A tempting mistake is to include 11 among satisfying primes without respecting its prior exclusion.
Checking several primes larger than 13 does not prove that every larger prime is excluded.
Showing that 17 is excluded does not by itself prove that 13 is the largest satisfying prime.
Arguing that large primes are likely to hit a nonsquare-free remainder is not a proof that all large primes fail.
The claim that 101 mod 13 equals 9 is a modular arithmetic error; 101 mod 13 equals 10.
Inferring that all primes greater than 13 fail from only several example failures is not a valid proof of the universal claim.
Relying only on the rapid growth of the denominators does not prove that every partial sum is less than 1.
Guessing a denominator pattern from the first few terms is not a proof unless the recurrence is derived.
Showing that the terms decrease quickly does not by itself establish a sharp upper bound for all partial sums.
A common pitfall is treating the partial-fraction identity as a consequence of the recurrence rather than as an algebraic identity.
It is not enough to use 10^φ(n) ≡ 1 mod n and conclude that n divides (10^φ(n)-1)/9.
Canceling a factor in modular arithmetic is invalid unless that factor is invertible modulo the modulus.
Forgetting the constant of integration prevents using the given point to determine the specific function.
Integrating x^-2 as a positive x^-1 term gives the wrong sign because division by -1 is required.
Do not reject a positive target minimum just because the given minimum is negative; the two minimized quadratics are different functions.
Multiplying or simplifying the minimum equation to -6b+6c-1=-19 is an algebra error and does not imply c=b-17/12.
Treating the triangle vertices as points lying on the original sides is wrong because the relevant vertex is the new third vertex of each equilateral triangle.
Leaving 'vertices of adjacent triangles' ambiguous makes it unclear which segments' midpoints are being studied.
Choosing a 60-degree rotation direction without matching the external side can place an equilateral triangle on the wrong side of the hexagon.
Assuming consecutive midpoint position vectors are simple 60-degree rotations about the origin gives a false coefficient identity.
Counting the single placement for n equals 1 as valid is wrong because that placement puts the letter in its designated envelope.
Accepting the correct placement is a pitfall when the goal is to avoid correct placements.
Assuming that correct individual mappings are sufficient to make the overall configuration valid is a pitfall.
Treating an implication as automatically reversible is a common invalid move.
Assuming a cycle of implications forces at least one proposition to be true is a wrong approach.
Counting A->C, B->B, C->A as a derangement is wrong because B is fixed.
Treating n!/e without rounding as an exact derangement count is wrong because n!/e is generally not an integer.
Rejecting choice C solely because 20/3 is not an integer ignores that the denominator may cancel with factors inside (19!)^2.
Testing only whether the visible multiplier 20/k is an integer square can obscure the needed prime-exponent parity check in the full expression.
Checking only the exponent of 2 can falsely suggest an option is a square when another prime still has an odd exponent.
Ignoring the prime factor removed by k can miss that division changes an exponent from even to odd.
It is wrong to conclude that every prime exponent in 19! is even because squaring doubles exponents; squaring affects (19!)^2, not 19! itself.
Assuming division by 1 can make the value a perfect square is wrong when an odd prime exponent remains.
Assuming division by 2 gives a perfect square is wrong when the resulting exponent of 2 is odd.
Treating a number as a perfect square despite an odd prime exponent is a misconception.
Checking only that the exponent of 2 becomes even is insufficient because another prime exponent may remain odd.
Assuming the two equal-product subsets must each contain three numbers is unjustified because equal products do not imply equal subset sizes.
Requiring one of the six numbers to equal p^2 is too narrow; the relevant condition is that the term divisible by p contain an even power of p.
Treating the presence of p^2 in the block as enough for square parity is wrong when another multiple of p also lies in the block.
A tempting wrong approach is to assume that including one prime square such as 49 is enough to make the total product a square.
A tempting wrong approach is to assume that a block of six composite numbers avoids the square-product obstruction.
A wrong approach is to search directly for equal subset products without first using the necessary square condition on the total product.
It is wrong to assume a prime at least 7 can have its exponent paired across two different numbers in a block of six consecutive integers.
Assuming that including p^2 for p >= 7 only fixes the exponent of p is wrong because neighboring numbers can introduce other primes with odd exponents.
Assuming prime exponents can be balanced across six consecutive numbers overlooks unavoidable odd prime exponents.
